title: The Viking look. The horned helmet was a costume designer's idea.
description:
The horned helmet was a costume designer's idea. Carl Emil Doepler's designs for an 1876 production of Wagner's Ring brought it to fame.

Viking helmet remains are known. The most complete, found in Norway in 1943 at Gjermundbu, shows no sign of ever having had horns.

Costume designer for the Ring premiere. He studied Viking Age artefacts in museums, then took artistic freedom.

Wings, not horns. The horned version grew from a mix of Norse and medieval German history.

Earlier Germanic tribes. Helmets of the Migration Period, 375 to 568 AD, fit the look better than anything Viking.

Painters ran with it. Lorenz Frolich's 1877 painting of Sweyn Forkbeard is described as the first known horned Viking in course literature.

The horns came from the theatre.

Sources:
- https://www.scandinavianarchaeology.com/?p=896 (read): established that the Gjermundbu helmet, c.875 AD from a male grave in Norway, shows no sign of ever having had horns; that Vendel period helmets (550 to 793 AD) have none either; that Carl Emil Doepler designed costumes for the 1876 premiere of Wagner's Ring, studied Viking Age artefacts and used artistic freedom, and gave Odin wings instead of horns; and that Lorenz Frolich's 1877 painting of Sweyn Forkbeard's capture is described as the first known illustration of a horned Viking in course literature.
- https://www.historyhit.com/types-of-viking-helmets/ (read): established that the Gjermundbu helmet was found in southern Norway in 1943, is iron with four plates and a fixed visor, and is the most complete of only five known Viking helmet remains; that the horned helmet was not worn by real Vikings; that Doepler's designs for an 1876 Ring production first showcased it; and that the look blended Norse and medieval German history, closer to Germanic tribes of the Migration Period (375 to 568 AD).
